items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a hypothesis (one-step operationalization with a comparison group)
items.passage: Psychologist Rachel E. White and colleagues asked four- and six-year-old children to work for 10 minutes on a repetitive computer task, telling them they could take breaks whenever they wished to play an appealing video game. Some children were instructed to think about how they themselves were doing on the task, while others were asked to pretend to be a hardworking character, such as Batman, as they worked. The researchers hypothesized that impersonating such a character would help children persevere.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ hypothesis?
options: Children who pretended to be a hardworking character such as Batman spent more time on the task than children who thought about themselves did.
Six-year-olds spent more time on the task than four-year-olds did, regardless of what they had been asked to think about.
Children who pretended to be Batman reported afterward that they had enjoyed the video game more than the task.
When asked to pretend to be a character, most of the children chose a superhero or other character that they had already seen in movies or on television.
items.explanation: The researchers hypothesized that “impersonating such a character would help children persevere.” If children who pretended to be a hardworking character kept working longer than children who thought about themselves, then impersonating the character helped them persevere, so choice A supports the hypothesis.

B.recipe: SUBJ: the right outcome compared by age, not by instruction
B.why_wrong: A difference between age groups says nothing about whether pretending to be a character helped children persevere.

C.recipe: OFF: enjoyment of the game, not time on task
C.why_wrong: Which activity the children enjoyed more does not show whether impersonating a character kept them working.

D.recipe: OFF: which characters were chosen
D.why_wrong: Where the children had seen their characters says nothing about how long they persevered at the task.

sources.what: White, Prager, Schaefer, Kross, Duckworth, Carlson 2017, Child Development 88(5): 1563-1571, The Batman Effect: 4- and 6-year-olds (N = 180) did a repetitive task for 10 minutes with the option to take breaks to play an attractive video game; children who impersonated an exemplar other such as Batman spent the most time working, then third-person self-talk, then first-person; 6-year-olds persevered longer than 4-year-olds

items.notes: Easy. Psychology. The key states the hypothesis's outcome (time on task) for the right comparison (character vs self). B is a true result of the study about age, not the hypothesis. The study's third condition (third-person self-talk) is left out for length. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Quotation from a participant illustrates a researcher’s two-part claim (soccer and community)
items.passage: The Mathare Youth Sports Association, founded in 1987 in Mathare, a group of informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya, organizes soccer leagues for thousands of young people. Teams earn points not only by winning matches but also by participating in projects to clear garbage from their neighborhoods. Based on interviews with players, a researcher claims that many young people valued the program because it allowed them to improve their community as well as to play soccer.
items.stem: Which quotation from a player would best illustrate the researcher’s claim?
options: “I joined because my older brother played on a team, and our team practiced every afternoon on a field close to my school.”
“The best part was traveling to matches in other parts of Nairobi and getting to meet players from neighborhoods I had never visited before.”
“Some of the clean-up days were hot and tiring, and honestly I only went to them because our team needed the points.”
“I came for the soccer, but I stayed because when we cleared the garbage from our street, people saw young people making Mathare better.”
items.explanation: The researcher claims that young people valued the program “because it allowed them to improve their community as well as to play soccer.” In choice D the player came for soccer but stayed because clearing garbage showed young people “making Mathare better,” which illustrates both parts of the claim.

A.recipe: OFF: why the player joined
A.why_wrong: It explains how the player came to the program but says nothing about valuing the chance to improve the community.

B.recipe: OFF: travel and new friends
B.why_wrong: It values meeting other players, not improving the player’s own community.

C.recipe: LURE: mentions the clean-ups but does not value them
C.why_wrong: The player took part in clean-ups only for the points, so the quotation does not show that improving the community was something the player valued.

sources.what: Mathare Youth Sports Association (MYSA), founded 1987 in Mathare, Nairobi, by Bob Munro; football leagues for thousands of children (14,000 in 1,200 teams in 2010); teams score points for participating in clean-up projects as well as for matches won; UNEP Global 500 award 1999

items.notes: Easy. Sociology. The researcher and the players' quotations are unnamed and invented, as in CB's participant items; the program facts are real. C is the lure: clean-ups mentioned, but valued only for points. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: D, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Data completion (the row that is the extreme in two columns at once)
items.passage: Between the 1960s and the 1980s, many British colonies in the Caribbean became independent nations. A student compiling information about five of these countries notices that the country that gained independence most recently is also the smallest of the five in area. That country is ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: Grenada.
Saint Kitts and Nevis.
Dominica.
Barbados.

table.title: Independence and Area of Five Caribbean Countries
columns: Year of independence from the United Kingdom

items.explanation: The country must have the latest year of independence and the smallest area. Saint Kitts and Nevis became independent in 1983, later than any other country in the table, and its area of 261 square kilometers is the smallest shown, so choice B completes the statement.

A.recipe: WGRP: the second smallest
A.why_wrong: Grenada (344 square kilometers) is larger than Saint Kitts and Nevis, and it became independent earlier, in 1974.

C.recipe: WDIR: the largest
C.why_wrong: Dominica, at 750 square kilometers, is the largest of the five countries, and it became independent in 1978.

D.recipe: WDIR: the earliest
D.why_wrong: Barbados became independent earliest, in 1966, not most recently.

sources.what: Independence dates and areas (Wikipedia infoboxes): Barbados 30 November 1966, 439 km2; Grenada 7 February 1974, 344 km2; Dominica 3 November 1978, 750 km2; Saint Lucia 22 February 1979, 617 km2; Saint Kitts and Nevis 19 September 1983, 261 km2

items.notes: Easy. History/geography. The extreme in two columns at once (latest year, smallest area), like CB 1.23. Each country's figures from its Wikipedia infobox, checked 2026-10-27. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a single-trait claim (a character reasoning only from what it has seen; poem)
items.passage: “The Tendril’s Fate” is a 1901 poem by Ella Wheeler Wilcox. In the poem, a sprout buried beneath the snow sings about the coming spring while objects around it ridicule its song. Wilcox portrays one of the sprout’s critics as mistaking the limits of its own experience for the limits of the world: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from “The Tendril’s Fate” most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “‘How foolish your songs!’ said a lump of clay; / ‘What is there, I ask, to prove them? / Just look at the walls between you and the day, / Now, have you the strength to move them?’”
“Under the snow, in the dark and the cold, / A pale little sprout was humming; / Sweetly it sang, ’neath the frozen mould, / Of the beautiful days that were coming.”
“A pebble spoke next: ‘You are quite absurd,’ / It said, ‘with your song’s insistence; / For I never saw a tree or a bird, / So of course there are none in existence.’”
“‘But I know, I know,’ the tendril cried, / In beautiful sweet unreason; / Till lo! from its prison, glorified, / It burst in the glad spring season.”
items.explanation: The claim is that one critic mistakes the limits of its own experience for the limits of the world. In choice C the pebble reasons, “I never saw a tree or a bird, / So of course there are none in existence”: because it has not seen such things, it concludes they do not exist.

A.recipe: OFF: a critic who doubts for a different reason
A.why_wrong: The clay mocks the sprout by pointing to the walls around it and its lack of strength, an argument about obstacles, not one based on what the clay has never seen.

B.recipe: SUBJ: the sprout, not a critic
B.why_wrong: These lines describe the sprout singing hopefully, not any critic’s reasoning.

D.recipe: SUBJ: the sprout’s confidence and the outcome
D.why_wrong: These lines show the sprout’s certainty and its emergence in spring; they do not show a critic judging the world by its own experience.

sources.what: Ella Wheeler Wilcox, The Tendril's Fate, in Poems of Power (Chicago: W. B. Conkey, copyright 1901; Gutenberg text from the London Gay and Hancock edition); all four stanzas checked as exact text, with inner double quotes rendered as single quotes and the italic I set roman

items.notes: Easy. Poem. Single-trait claim about the pebble; the clay is the other critic with a different argument. The collection's copyright pages (archive.org scan, poemsofpower00wilc) show 1901, 1902 and 1903; the poem is in the earliest edition scanned. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.

review.notes: all four stanzas exact against Gutenberg 6667 (inner double quotes as single, italic I set roman).

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a proposed pattern of selective sickness behavior (valuable interactions kept, less valuable ones dropped)
items.passage: When an animal mounts an immune response to an infection, it often becomes lethargic and withdraws from its social group, a set of changes known as sickness behavior. Withdrawal carries costs, however, particularly for gregarious species whose members depend on one another. Common vampire bats (Desmodus rotundus) that fail to obtain a blood meal can starve within days unless a roostmate regurgitates blood for them, whereas mutual grooming, though frequent, contributes less directly to survival. Sebastian Stockmaier and colleagues injected vampire bats with a compound that stimulates an immune response without causing an infection, and they propose that sickness curtails least those of a bat’s social interactions that contribute most to its survival.
items.stem: Which finding from the study, if true, would most directly support Stockmaier and colleagues’ proposal?
options: Injected bats made fewer contact calls to their roostmates than they had before the injection, and the calls they did make tended to be shorter.
After the injection, the bats groomed their roostmates less often than they had before, and they also interacted with fewer roostmates overall.
Injected bats still received regurgitated blood from roostmates about as often as before, even as the grooming they received fell sharply.
Injected bats spent more of each night resting alone in the roost than uninjected bats did, and they also left the roost to forage less often.
items.explanation: The researchers propose that sickness “curtails least those of a bat’s social interactions that contribute most to its survival.” The text explains that receiving regurgitated blood can keep a bat from starving, “whereas mutual grooming, though frequent, contributes less directly to survival.” If injected bats still received food about as often as before while the grooming they received fell sharply, the more valuable interaction was preserved while the less valuable one declined, which is the pattern the proposal predicts.

A.recipe: OFF: another social behavior, no comparison of value
A.why_wrong: Fewer and shorter contact calls show that the bats became less social, but the finding does not compare an interaction that matters for survival with one that matters less.

B.recipe: TRAP: a general decline consistent with any account of sickness behavior
B.why_wrong: A drop in grooming and in the number of partners is what ordinary sickness behavior predicts; it says nothing about whether the bats kept up the interactions that matter most, such as food sharing.

D.recipe: TRAP: lethargy shown, but no interaction is compared
D.why_wrong: Resting alone and foraging less show that the bats were lethargic, which any account of sickness behavior expects; the finding does not show which interactions the bats preserved.

sources.what: Stockmaier, Bolnick, Page, Carter 2020, J Anim Ecol 89(6):1387-1394: LPS immune challenge in common vampire bats; effects of sickness should be lower for behaviours with greater fitness benefits such as food sharing; immune-challenged bats had a greater reduction in allogrooming received than in food sharing received

items.notes: Band 6. Life science (animal behavior). Two linked steps: the passage ranks food sharing above grooming for survival, and the key must be read as the valuable interaction kept while the less valuable one fell. Real result recast as a hypothetical finding. B and D look like evidence of sickness behavior but cannot separate the proposal from plain lethargy; A is the bats' contact calls (a real separate finding by the same group, Stockmaier et al. 2020 Biol Lett), which compare nothing. The study's kin result is left out of the passage to keep one claim. Starvation within a few days without a shared meal is the well-known premise from Wilkinson's work, stated loosely.

band7.why: Two steps: the passage ranks food sharing above grooming for survival and the key must be read as the valuable interaction kept while the less valuable one fell. B and D are TRAPs consistent with plain sickness behavior, A is OFF. The key is the only option naming food sharing, which keeps it at the easy end of band 6; a food-sharing decoy tried in review made D partly supportive, so it was not kept. Planned 6.

fixes: proposal reworded ("sickness curtails least those of a bat’s social interactions") so the key’s received food and grooming fit it; explanation quote updated

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a chronological claim (fortification did not follow a state collapse at once)
items.passage: During the Late Intermediate Period (roughly 1000–1450 CE), communities across much of the Andean highlands abandoned fertile valley floors for fortified settlements on hilltops and ridges, known as pukaras. Archaeologists traditionally attributed this relocation to warfare that erupted as a direct consequence of the collapse, around 1000 CE, of Tiwanaku and Wari, the states that had dominated the region in preceding centuries. After obtaining radiocarbon dates for the construction and occupation of pukaras in the northern Lake Titicaca Basin, however, archaeologist Elizabeth Arkush concluded that the proliferation of these hilltop fortifications was not an immediate consequence of that collapse.
items.stem: Which finding about the northern Lake Titicaca Basin, if true, would most directly support Arkush’s conclusion?
options: Most villages occupied in the region during the two centuries after 1000 CE stood on low, open ground near farmland and had no surrounding walls.
Many of the region’s pukaras were abandoned and later reoccupied, and the walls of several were rebuilt more than once over the following centuries.
Some of the earliest walls at the region’s pukaras were built with stone blocks taken from Tiwanaku buildings soon after those buildings fell into disuse.
Pukaras built elsewhere in the Andes after 1300 CE were enclosed by walls of the same height and thickness as those found in the region.
items.explanation: Arkush concluded that “the proliferation of these hilltop fortifications was not an immediate consequence of that collapse,” which occurred “around 1000 CE.” If, in the two centuries after 1000 CE, most villages in the region stood on low, open ground without walls, then people were not yet moving to defended hilltops in the period right after the collapse, so the shift to pukaras came later, as Arkush concluded.

B.recipe: TRAP: true of the sites but silent on when fortification began
B.why_wrong: Cycles of abandonment, reoccupation, and rebuilding say nothing about when people first began building pukaras, so the finding cannot show whether that happened right after the collapse.

C.recipe: OPP: early walls built right after the collapse
C.why_wrong: Walls built from Tiwanaku stone soon after its buildings fell out of use would suggest that fortification began shortly after the collapse, which runs against Arkush’s conclusion.

D.recipe: OFF: wall construction elsewhere, not timing in the basin
D.why_wrong: Similar wall dimensions in other parts of the Andes say nothing about when pukaras appeared in the northern Lake Titicaca Basin relative to the collapse.

sources.what: Arkush 2008, Latin American Antiquity 19(4), War, Chronology, and Causality in the Titicaca Basin: traditional assumption that Late Intermediate Period warfare resulted directly from the collapse of Wari and Tiwanaku around AD 1000; radiocarbon dates from northern Titicaca Basin pukaras show hillforts did not become common until after about AD 1300

items.notes: Band 6. Archaeology. Two steps: settlement location and the absence of walls stand for the absence of fortification, and the time window must be the one right after the collapse. Real core claim (abstract read via OpenAlex; Crossref confirms author and journal). The key paraphrases the claim through an observable pattern the passage does not mention. B uses the abstract's own reoccupation cycles, which cannot date the start. C is the reversed timing. D compares wall form elsewhere.

band7.why: Two steps: open, unwalled villages stand for the absence of fortification, and the window must be the one right after the collapse. C is the reversed timing (OPP), B a TRAP true of the sites but silent on the start. Planned 6.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a proposed physical mechanism; the key supplies an unstated premise (a race between sinking and upward ice flow)
items.passage: Parts of Antarctica are among the most productive places on Earth for finding meteorites. Meteorites that land on the ice sheet are transported within the flowing ice, and in some zones, where the ice moves upward and its surface is continually eroded, they emerge and accumulate on the surface. Yet iron-rich meteorites constitute a much smaller proportion of the meteorites recovered from these zones than of those recovered elsewhere. Sunlight can penetrate the ice to a depth of a few tens of centimeters. Mathematicians and earth scientists at the University of Manchester propose that it warms meteorites buried at those depths and that iron-rich ones, which conduct heat efficiently, melt the ice beneath them and sink, possibly as rapidly as the ice carries them upward.
items.stem: Which finding about Antarctic meteorite collection zones, if true, would most directly support the explanation proposed by the scientists at the University of Manchester?
options: Iron-rich meteorites that land on the ice sheet are more likely than other meteorites to break apart on impact into fragments too small for searchers to notice.
Meteorites of every type are found in greater numbers in the zones where the surface of the ice is worn away fastest than in the zones where it is worn away slowly.
During the Antarctic summer, sunlight passes into the ice of the collection zones to a depth of several tens of centimeters before it is fully absorbed.
Iron-rich meteorites make up a larger share of the finds in zones where the ice rises toward the surface unusually quickly than in zones where it rises slowly.
items.explanation: The scientists propose that iron-rich meteorites “melt the ice beneath them and sink, possibly as rapidly as the ice carries them upward.” If sinking competes with the upward movement of the ice, then where the ice rises unusually quickly the sinking should be less able to keep pace, so more iron-rich meteorites should reach the surface there. A larger share of iron-rich finds in fast-rising zones than in slow-rising ones is exactly the pattern the explanation predicts, and an explanation unrelated to sinking would not predict it.

A.recipe: OPP: a rival explanation (breakup on impact, a collection bias)
A.why_wrong: If iron-rich meteorites shatter into unnoticeable fragments, their scarcity would have a cause that has nothing to do with sinking, which undercuts the team’s explanation rather than supporting it.

B.recipe: TRAP: consistent with any account, the general concentration process
B.why_wrong: More meteorites of every type where the surface wears away fastest only reflects how meteorites in general are brought to the surface; it does not bear on why iron-rich ones in particular are scarce.

C.recipe: GEN: restates the premise the explanation already assumes
C.why_wrong: The text already states that sunlight “can penetrate the ice to a depth of a few tens of centimeters”; confirming that depth says nothing about whether iron-rich meteorites actually sink as fast as the ice rises.

sources.what: Evatt, Coughlan, Joy, Smedley, Connolly, Abrahams 2016, Nature Communications 7:10679 (University of Manchester): iron and stony-iron meteorites under-represented in Antarctic stranding zones where upward-flowing ice and ablation concentrate meteorites; englacial solar warming melts surrounding ice for meteorites a few tens of centimetres below the surface; high thermal conductivity (iron) meteorites can sink at a rate sufficient to offset the annual upward ice transport

items.notes: Band 7. Earth and space science. Three steps: the explanation is a race between sinking and upward flow; the passage never mentions that upward speed differs between zones; where the ice rises faster, irons should surface more. Lead author named as a team (his first name could not be confirmed on a fetched page; affiliation is in the PubMed record). Different concept from the live Transitions item on ANSMET curation (transitions.U1_culmination_alt.medium.w3b4_13): that item is about storing meteorites, not their scarcity. Stem 20 words, names the claimant.
band7_moves: key supplies an unstated premise (upward ice speed varies between zones, so the race can be lost)
TRAP B consistent with any account of how meteorites surface
OPP A is a rival explanation (collection bias)
GEN C restates the assumed premise
stem narrows the finding and names the claimant

band7.why: Three steps: the key supplies the unstated premise that upward ice speed varies between zones, so sinking can lose the race where ice rises fast. TRAP B fits any account of how meteorites surface, OPP A is a rival collection bias, GEN C restates a stated fact. Stem 20 words names the claimants; passage about 125 words.

fixes: penetration depth moved out of the proposal into a stated fact, so C is a clean restatement (GEN) rather than partial support for the proposal
C why_wrong misquoted the passage ("a few tens of centimeters down"); now quotes it word for word

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding discriminates between two explanations (capital shortage vs uninsured risk); the key is a difference that only one explanation predicts
items.passage: Small-scale farmers in many low-income regions invest little in fertilizer and other agricultural inputs even when such investments would, on average, be highly profitable. Economists have proposed two explanations: some argue that farmers simply lack access to cash or credit, while others contend that farmers avoid investing because a drought could destroy the harvest and leave them unable to recover the expense. To evaluate these explanations, Dean Karlan and colleagues conducted experiments in northern Ghana in which they randomly offered some farmers cash grants, some insurance that pays out when rainfall is low, and some both. The researchers concluded that uninsured risk, rather than a shortage of capital, was the principal obstacle to investment.
items.stem: Which finding from the experiments, if true, would most directly support Karlan and colleagues’ conclusion?
options: Farmers who received only cash grants increased their spending on fertilizer and other inputs by more than farmers who received only rainfall insurance did.
Farmers given only rainfall insurance raised their spending on inputs by about as much as farmers given both insurance and a cash grant did.
Farmers who received both rainfall insurance and a cash grant spent more on fertilizer and other inputs than farmers who received neither one did.
Farmers whose insurance paid out after a season of poor rain were more likely than other insured farmers to buy rainfall insurance again the following year.
items.explanation: The researchers concluded that “uninsured risk, rather than a shortage of capital, was the principal obstacle to investment.” If farmers who received only insurance raised their spending about as much as farmers who received insurance plus cash, then once the risk was covered, extra money added almost nothing to investment. That pattern is what the risk explanation predicts and what the cash-shortage explanation does not, since under that view the added grant should have raised spending further.

A.recipe: OPP: the rival view’s prediction (cash matters more than insurance)
A.why_wrong: If cash alone raised spending more than insurance alone, a shortage of money would look like the bigger obstacle, which is the view the researchers rejected.

C.recipe: TRAP: fits both explanations
C.why_wrong: Farmers given both cash and insurance would be expected to spend more than farmers given nothing under either explanation, so the finding cannot show which obstacle matters more.

D.recipe: OFF: a true property of the insurance (repurchase after payouts), irrelevant to the obstacle
D.why_wrong: Whether farmers buy insurance again after a payout concerns demand for insurance, not whether risk or a lack of money held back their spending on farm inputs.

sources.what: Karlan, Osei, Osei-Akoto, Udry 2014, Quarterly Journal of Economics 129(2):597-652, Agricultural Decisions after Relaxing Credit and Risk Constraints: randomized cash grants, rainfall index insurance, or both in northern Ghana; insurance leads to significantly larger agricultural investment; the binding constraint is uninsured risk; demand for insurance rises with the farmer's own receipt of payouts

items.notes: Band 7. Economics. The key is a difference of conditions (insurance only vs insurance plus cash) whose equality only the risk view predicts; the student must see that the added cash is the test of the rival view. D is a real finding from the abstract that bears on demand, not on the obstacle. Different concept from live Karlan items (matching grants; Gine and Karlan group liability) and from the Uganda YOP cash-grants item. Stem names the claimant.
band7_moves: key is an unexpected route (the cash grant adds nothing once risk is insured)
TRAP C fits both explanations
OPP A is the rival's prediction
D is a true but irrelevant property of the same insurance
stem narrows the finding to the experiments and names the claimant

band7.why: Discrimination: the risk view predicts insurance only about equal to insurance plus cash, the capital view predicts the cash adds more, so the key splits them through an unexpected route (the grant adds nothing once risk is covered). TRAP C (both > neither) fits both views; OPP A is the rival prediction; D is a true but irrelevant property of the insurance. Stem names the study and claimants; passage 114 words.

items.subtype: Data description: interaction (which animal group removes the most seeds depends on the stage)
items.passage: Seed-eating animals can remove seeds at two distinct stages: before dispersal, while the fruits remain attached to the parent plant, or after dispersal, once the seeds have fallen to the ground. Working in a tropical desert in Mexico, a team of Mexican ecologists investigated seed removal from Stenocereus stellatus, a columnar cactus whose fleshy fruits are eaten by many animals, using experimental enclosures that admitted particular kinds of animals while excluding others. The team concluded that the animals responsible for most of the seed removal differed between the two stages.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the team’s conclusion?
options: All three groups of animals removed a greater percentage of seeds after the seeds had fallen to the ground than they removed while the fruits were still on the plant.
Birds removed a greater percentage of the seeds than rodents did, both while the fruits were still attached to the plant and after the seeds had fallen to the ground.
Before dispersal, birds removed a greater percentage of seeds than ants or rodents did, whereas after dispersal, ants removed a greater percentage than birds or rodents did.
Before dispersal, ants removed a greater percentage of the seeds than birds did, whereas after dispersal, birds removed a greater percentage of the seeds than ants did.

table.title: Percentage of Stenocereus stellatus Seeds Removed by Three Groups of Animals
table.note: Ranges give the lowest and highest values the researchers reported.

items.explanation: The team concluded that “the animals responsible for most of the seed removal differed between the two stages.” The table shows that before dispersal birds removed 10–28 percent of seeds, more than ants (2 percent) or rodents (1–4 percent), while after dispersal ants removed 62–64 percent, more than birds (34–38 percent) or rodents (16–30 percent). So the leading remover was birds at one stage and ants at the other, as choice C states.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but a change shared by all groups
A.why_wrong: Every group did remove more seeds after dispersal, but that is true of all three groups and says nothing about which group removed the most at each stage.

B.recipe: PART: accurate comparison of two groups that never changes
B.why_wrong: Birds did outremove rodents at both stages, but a comparison that stays the same across stages cannot show that the leading remover changed; it also leaves out ants, the leaders after dispersal.

D.recipe: INACC: both comparisons reversed
D.why_wrong: Before dispersal ants removed only 2 percent of seeds, fewer than birds (10–28 percent), and after dispersal ants (62–64 percent) removed more than birds (34–38 percent), so both halves misread the table.

sources.what: Alvarez-Espino, Rios-Casanova, Godinez-Alvarez 2017, Plant Biology 19(3):469-474 (FES Iztacala, UNAM), Seed removal in a tropical North American desert: selective exclosures for Stenocereus stellatus; pre-dispersal removal by birds 10-28%, ants 2%, rodents 1-4%; post-dispersal removal by ants 62-64%, birds 34-38%, rodents 16-30%; birds and ants the main pre- and post-dispersal removers

items.notes: Band 6. Life science (ecology). Interaction of animal group and stage; the key needs four comparisons across two columns. Ranges exactly as in the abstract (the paper reports ranges, presumably across samplings). A and B are accurate but insufficient; D reverses both comparisons. Researchers' given names are only initials on PubMed, so the passage names the team by institution.

band7.why: Interaction across two columns: four comparisons to verify that the leading remover changes. A and B are accurate but insufficient, D reverses both halves. Planned 6.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates an indirect claim about a speaker's perception (poem)
items.passage: “Mnemosyne” is a 1902 poem by Trumbull Stickney. In the poem, the speaker revisits in imagination the countryside where he once lived and finds it profoundly transformed. He suggests that the countryside has grown so desolate that its condition would bewilder him if it were not so familiar: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from “Mnemosyne” most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “But that I knew these places are my own, / I’d ask how came such wretchedness to cumber / The earth, and I to people it alone.”
“It’s dark about the country I remember. / There are the mountains where I lived. The path / Is slushed with cattle-tracks and fallen timber. / The stumps are twisted by the tempests’ wrath.”
“It’s lonely in the country I remember. / The babble of our children fills my ears. / And on our hearth I stare the perished ember / To flames that show all starry thro’ my tears.”
“It’s empty down the country I remember. / I had a sister lovely in my sight: / Her hair was dark, her eyes were very sombre; / We sang together in the woods at night.”
items.explanation: The claim is that the countryside has grown so bleak that the speaker would be baffled by it if it were not so familiar to him. In choice A, the speaker says that “But that I knew these places are my own,” he would wonder how “such wretchedness” came to “cumber / The earth”: only his prior knowledge tells him that this wretched landscape is his home.

B.recipe: HALF: the landscape is ruined, but he recognizes it at once
B.why_wrong: The speaker describes a ruined path and twisted stumps, but he identifies the scene immediately (“There are the mountains where I lived”); nothing suggests that he would be baffled by what he sees.

C.recipe: near emotion: grief over a lost family
C.why_wrong: The speaker mourns the family he remembers at his hearth, but the lines say nothing about the condition of the place baffling him.

D.recipe: near emotion: loss of a person, not of a recognizable place
D.why_wrong: The speaker recalls a sister and their singing, which conveys loss, but not that the countryside has become hard to recognize.

sources.what: text of Mnemosyne in Trumbull Stickney, Dramatic Verses (Boston: Charles E. Goodspeed, 1902), the year in the source line
same text in The Poems of Trumbull Stickney (1905), used for exact wording and punctuation

items.notes: Band 6. Literature (poem, 1902; author and work used in no official item or live item; Aby Warburg's Mnemosyne atlas in WiC w4b6_04 is a different work sharing only the title word). Quotations copied from the 1905 Poems OCR and checked against the 1902 OCR (the 1902 scan has OCR noise; wording agrees). Claim verb indirect (suggests); B is the hard half-match, the ruined landscape recognized at once. Option A is three lines, a sentence-boundary trim of the sixth stanza.

band7.why: Indirect claim verb (suggests) and a counterfactual; B is the close half-match from the same stanza (ruin plus recognition, no bewilderment), C and D nearby emotions. Planned 6.

items.subtype: Quotation from a critic supports a historians' claim about an artist's institutional legacy
items.passage: Daphne Odjig, an artist of Odawa, Potawatomi, and English descent, is celebrated for paintings that combine the curving, emphatically outlined forms of Indigenous pictographs with the fragmented, overlapping planes of European cubism. In 1971 she established a small print shop in Winnipeg, Manitoba, and by 1974 she and her husband had expanded it into the New Warehouse Gallery, the first gallery in Canada devoted exclusively to First Nations art. Some art historians contend that the gallery was as consequential for Indigenous art in Canada as Odjig’s own paintings were.
items.stem: Which quotation from an art critic would best support the claim of the art historians mentioned in the text?
options: “The New Warehouse Gallery was a modest business; what changed Canadian art was Odjig’s painting itself, whose interlocking, brightly colored figures showed viewers that Anishinaabe imagery could carry the ambitions of modern art.”
“Odjig’s New Warehouse Gallery was the first in Canada to show First Nations art exclusively, and it was also the country’s first art gallery to be owned and operated by an Indigenous artist.”

“Whether she was painting legends from Manitoulin Island or illustrating traditional stories, Odjig returned again and again to the narratives of her community, treating each work as a way of preserving them.”

“When most Canadian galleries still treated First Nations work as craft, Odjig’s gallery let Indigenous painters exhibit and sell as contemporary artists, building an audience on which many of their careers came to depend.”
items.explanation: The art historians “contend that the gallery was as consequential for Indigenous art in Canada as Odjig’s own paintings were.” Choice D credits the gallery with an effect beyond Odjig’s own work: it gave Indigenous painters a place to exhibit and sell as contemporary artists and built the audience their careers depended on, which is the kind of broad importance the historians claim for it.

A.recipe: OPP: sides with the view the historians push against (the paintings mattered more)
A.why_wrong: This critic calls the gallery “a modest business” and credits the change in Canadian art to the paintings, which runs against the historians’ claim.

B.recipe: HALF: the gallery’s firsts, with no effect on Indigenous art
B.why_wrong: The quotation records what made the gallery unusual but says nothing about what it did for other artists or for Indigenous art in Canada, so it does not show that it mattered as much as the paintings.

C.recipe: OFF: the subjects of her paintings
C.why_wrong: The quotation concerns the stories Odjig painted, not the gallery or its importance.

sources.what: Daphne Odjig: Odawa-Potawatomi-English artist; pictographic/Woodlands style with cubist influence, curving contours and strong outlining; opened Odjig Indian Prints of Canada in Winnipeg in 1971; by 1974 she and her husband expanded it into the New Warehouse Gallery, the first Canadian gallery exclusively representing First Nations art and the first Native-owned gallery; illustrated Tales from the Smokehouse; painted Manitoulin legends

items.notes: Band 6. Arts. Quotations are invented and attributed to an unnamed critic, as in the official items; their facts follow the source (B's firsts, C's subjects). The historians' claim is a comparison (as much as the paintings), so D must show a broad effect of the gallery; B is the strongest wrong option, true facts about the gallery with no effect named. Odjig appears in no official or live item.

band7.why: The claim is a comparison of consequence; B gives true firsts with no effect named, A sides with the paintings, C is off-target. Quotations under 40 words. Planned 6.

items.subtype: Data completion: condition vs control with a filter column; the expected protective effect fails and the key needs both conditions
items.passage: Raccoons excavate and consume the eggs of many freshwater turtles that bury their clutches in sandy riverbanks. Because a nesting turtle leaves conspicuous disturbances on the surface of the sand, some researchers have proposed that raccoons locate nests visually and that sweeping away those markings could protect the eggs. At two nesting sites of map turtles along the lower Wisconsin River, researcher Gregory A. Geller swept some nesting areas with brooms, and he also constructed artificial nests, some consisting of an excavated and refilled cavity without eggs and others consisting only of imitation surface markings. His results suggested that the markings were neither necessary nor sufficient for raccoons to locate a nest: ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: raccoons disturbed every one of the turtle nests in areas that had been swept, a slightly higher percentage than the percentage of turtle nests they disturbed in areas that had not been swept.
raccoons disturbed at least 95 percent of the nests with cavities whether or not the area had been swept but only about a quarter of the imitation marks, which lacked a cavity.

raccoons disturbed only about a quarter of the imitation surface marks, which had no cavity beneath them, far fewer than the percentage of artificial nests with cavities that they disturbed in unswept areas.

raccoons disturbed a slightly smaller percentage of the artificial nests in swept areas than of those in unswept areas, which suggests that removing the surface marks gives nests at least some protection.

table.title: Percentage of Nests and Imitation Marks Disturbed by Raccoons within 24 Hours

items.explanation: The statement says the markings “were neither necessary nor sufficient for raccoons to locate a nest,” so the data must show two things. Raccoons found nests without marks: they disturbed 100 percent of turtle nests and 95 percent of artificial nests in swept areas, about the same rates as in unswept areas. And marks alone rarely drew them: only 26 percent of the imitation marks, which had no cavity, were disturbed. Choice B reports both patterns.

A.recipe: PART: accurate, shows only that the marks were not necessary
A.why_wrong: The swept turtle nests show that raccoons could find nests without marks, but the choice says nothing about the imitation marks, so it does not show that the marks alone were insufficient.

C.recipe: HALF: accurate, shows only that the marks were not sufficient
C.why_wrong: The low rate for the imitation marks shows that marks alone rarely drew raccoons, but the comparison uses unswept nests, which had marks, so it does not show that raccoons could find nests without them.

D.recipe: CONTRA: an accurate small difference used to argue the opposite
D.why_wrong: The drop from 100 to 95 percent is real, but treating it as protection contradicts the statement, and raccoons still disturbed nearly all the swept nests.

sources.what: Geller 2015, Chelonian Conservation and Biology 14(1):64-72, A Test of Substrate Sweeping as a Strategy to Reduce Raccoon Predation of Freshwater Turtle Nests: Graptemys nesting sites on the lower Wisconsin River 2013-2014; natural nests depredated within 24 h, 95% unswept (n = 20) and 100% swept (n = 16); artificial nests with refilled cavities and no egg cues 100% unswept (n = 20) and 95% swept (n = 19); facsimiles of surface marks without cavities disturbed 26% (n = 19); cues not primarily visual

items.notes: Band 7. Life science (predator behavior). The passage relation (neither necessary nor sufficient) must be translated into two tests on the table; A and C each pass one test and are accurate readings, D is an accurate cell difference turned against the claim. Percentages and sample sizes from the abstract (read via OpenAlex; Crossref confirms author and journal). Option mean about 32 words. Different concept from the live Inferences item on raccoons and dog-bark playbacks and from the TSP item on decoy sea turtle eggs.
band7_moves: passage relation (neither necessary nor sufficient) applied to the display before the key follows
filter columns (swept, cavity) like the host column in 3.38
two accurate distractors each satisfying one half (PART, HALF)
CONTRA built from an accurate small difference
compound options of about 30 words

band7.why: Proxy: "neither necessary nor sufficient" must be turned into two tests on the table before the key follows; filter columns (swept, cavity); A and C are accurate and each pass one test; D is an accurate small difference turned against the claim; options about 32 words; passage 113 words; a surprise against the stated expectation that sweeping protects.

items.subtype: Data description: quantified claim over every time point (one series below two others at every point after the baseline)
items.passage: The Living Planet Index, compiled by the World Wildlife Fund and the Zoological Society of London, measures the average change in the size of thousands of monitored vertebrate populations relative to their size in 1970, which is assigned a value of 100. Separate indexes are calculated for populations living on land (terrestrial), in the ocean (marine), and in freshwater habitats such as rivers, lakes, and wetlands. Examining these indexes, a student concludes that freshwater populations have fared worse than both terrestrial and marine populations, not only in recent years but throughout the period since 1970.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the student’s conclusion?
options: In every year shown after 1970, the freshwater index was lower than both the terrestrial index and the marine index.
In 2020, the freshwater index was about 16, lower than both the terrestrial index of about 32 and the marine index of about 42.
In every year shown after 1970, the terrestrial index was lower than the marine index, and the freshwater index was lower than both of them.
All three indexes were lower in 2020 than in 1970, and none of the three indexes rose from any year shown to the next one.

figure.title: Living Planet Index for Terrestrial, Marine, and Freshwater Populations, 1970–2020
figure.description: Three lines at 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020; y-axis 0 to 100 in steps of 5. Terrestrial: 100, about 80, about 78, about 62, about 41, about 32. Marine: 100, about 85, about 60, about 54, about 48, about 42. Freshwater: 100, about 75, about 50, about 29, about 19, about 16. After 1970 the freshwater line is the lowest of the three at every point; the terrestrial line is above the marine line in 1990 and 2000 and below it in 1980, 2010 and 2020.

items.explanation: The student concludes that freshwater populations have fared worse “not only in recent years but throughout the period since 1970.” The graph shows that at every point after 1970 (1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020) the freshwater line lies below both the terrestrial line and the marine line, which is what choice A states.

B.recipe: PART: accurate, a single recent year
B.why_wrong: The 2020 values are read correctly, but one recent year cannot show that freshwater populations fared worse throughout the period, which is the point of the conclusion.

C.recipe: INACC: one clause false (terrestrial above marine in 1990 and 2000)
C.why_wrong: The terrestrial index was higher than the marine index in 1990 (about 78 vs. about 60) and in 2000 (about 62 vs. about 54), so the first part of this choice is false.

D.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but true of all three systems
D.why_wrong: All three indexes did decline at every step, but a decline shared by every system does not show that freshwater populations fared worse than the others.

sources.what: Living Planet Index by system, 1970-2020 values (terrestrial, marine, freshwater) from WWF and ZSL Living Planet Index data, latest edition, as published by Our World in Data (grapher living-planet-index-by-region, entities Terrestrial, Marine, Freshwater), checked 2026-10-27

items.notes: Band 6. Life science/environment. Quantified claim over time points (for every year after 1970), a different shape and display from b1's five-region table. Values from the OWID CSV for the current WWF/ZSL edition (1970 = 100), rounded on the graph; the 1980 gap between freshwater (about 75) and terrestrial (about 80) is half a gridline, so the key does not depend on reading it precisely beyond its order, which the description states. Living Planet Index is used by no other item.

band7.why: Quantified claim over every time point; B is the accurate single-year PART, D an accurate change shared by all, C one false clause. Planned 6 (CB has one band-7 Q2_P8 quantifier item).

items.subtype: Data completion: group membership stated in the passage applied to the display (members of one group differ)
items.passage: The rare earth elements, a group of metals that includes cerium, lanthanum, neodymium, and samarium, have uses ranging from powerful magnets to the polishing of precision lenses. They are classed together because their chemical properties are generally similar. Despite the group’s name, the US Geological Survey notes, its more abundant members are each about as common in Earth’s continental crust as familiar industrial metals such as copper, which is not a rare earth element. Similar chemistry does not mean similar abundance, however. Estimates of the crust’s average composition show that members of the group can differ considerably in how plentiful they are: ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
options: cerium, a rare earth element, is slightly more abundant in the crust than copper, which is not one, at about 66 and about 60 parts per million, respectively.
copper, which is not a rare earth element, is more than eight times as abundant in the crust as samarium, which is one, at about 60 and about 7 parts per million, respectively.
cerium and samarium, both of which are rare earth elements, are present in the crust at about 66 and about 7 parts per million, respectively, a roughly ninefold difference.
lanthanum and neodymium, both of which are rare earth elements, are nearly equally abundant in the crust, at about 39 and about 42 parts per million, respectively.

figure.title: Estimated Average Abundance of Five Elements in Earth’s Continental Crust
figure.description: Five bars; y-axis 0 to 70 in steps of 10. Cerium about 66; copper about 60; lanthanum about 39; neodymium about 42; samarium about 7.

items.explanation: The statement claims that members of the rare earth group “can differ considerably in how plentiful they are.” According to the text, cerium, lanthanum, neodymium, and samarium all belong to the group, while copper “is not a rare earth element.” The graph shows cerium at about 66 parts per million and samarium at about 7, so two members of the same group differ roughly ninefold in abundance, as choice C states.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but a member compared with a nonmember (echoes the USGS point in the text)
A.why_wrong: Cerium is slightly more abundant than copper, as the text leads one to expect, but copper is not a rare earth element, so the comparison says nothing about differences among members of the group.

B.recipe: IRREL: accurate, a large difference across categories
B.why_wrong: Copper is more than eight times as abundant as samarium, but copper is not a rare earth element, so this is not a difference between members of the same group.

D.recipe: IRREL: accurate sameness within the group offered as evidence of difference
D.why_wrong: Lanthanum and neodymium are both rare earth elements and do have similar abundances, but two members with nearly equal abundances illustrate similarity, the opposite of the statement.

sources.what: USGS Fact Sheet 087-02 (2002), Rare Earth Elements: Critical Resources for High Technology: the REE are generally similar in their geochemical properties, but their individual abundances are by no means equal; the more abundant REE are each similar in crustal concentration to commonplace industrial metals such as copper and lead; uses include magnets, and precision lenses are finished with cerium oxide

Abundance of elements in Earth’s crust, CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics 97th ed. values as tabulated on Wikipedia, checked 2026-10-27: cerium 66.5 ppm, copper 60, neodymium 41.5, lanthanum 39, samarium 7.05

items.notes: Band 6. Physical science (geochemistry). Written by the reviewer: the Bartomeus pollinator-exclusion draft repeated the concept of live CoE items w3b4_07 (common bean, mesh exclusion) and w4b2_08 (tomatillo, enclosed flowers) and was the batch’s fifth hard life-science item. Same Q1_P67 design as the draft: the passage gives group membership, the bars give values, and only within-group comparisons count. All three wrong options are accurate readings: a member against a nonmember that echoes the USGS point (A), a large member-nonmember gap (B), and within-group sameness (D). Values are the CRC figures; the USGS fact sheet supplies the premise (similar chemistry, unequal abundance, the more abundant members about as common as copper) but not the numbers. Rare earth abundance is used in no other item.

band7.why: Passage membership applied to unlabeled bars; key needs two reads, a ratio and a membership check; all three distractors accurate (two cross-category, one within-group sameness). Planned 6.

fixes: subject replaced: pollinator-exclusion yield gains (Bartomeus 2014) repeated the concept of live CoE w3b4_07 and w4b2_08 and was the fifth hard life-science item; new item on rare earth crustal abundance (USGS FS 087-02, CRC values), same Q1_P67 design, key kept at C
claims.txt: WITHDRAWN line for the Bartomeus claim and a new claim appended

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (admits she cannot control a feeling; insists her love is undiminished)
items.passage: The Girl with the Green Eyes is a 1902 play by Clyde Fitch. Jinny Austin, a young and devoted wife, is tormented by unfounded suspicions about her husband, Jack. Late in the play, Jinny acknowledges that her jealousy is beyond her control, though she insists that it has never diminished her affection for him: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Girl with the Green Eyes most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “I do believe you, and I do trust you, and I will try not to be jealous again!”
“It tells me that my jealousy all along has been right, that I’ve been a fool to let you blind me!”
“Once the cruel idea has got hold of me it seems to have to work its way out! Everything gets red before me and I don’t seem to know what I say or do! It’s no excuse, I know.”
“I never for one minute stopped loving you better than everything else in my life, but no more than I could stop loving you could I stop or help being jealous!”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Jinny admits that her jealousy is beyond her control, and she insists that it has never diminished her affection for Jack. In choice D she says she “never for one minute stopped loving” Jack, which covers the second part, and that “no more than I could stop loving you could I stop or help being jealous,” which admits that the jealousy is beyond her control.

A.recipe: LURE: mentions jealousy, but as something she will try to stop
A.why_wrong: Jinny promises to try not to be jealous, which implies she thinks she can control it, and she says nothing about her love being undiminished.

B.recipe: OFF: jealousy defended as justified
B.why_wrong: Jinny claims her jealousy was right all along; she neither admits that she cannot control it nor speaks of her love.

C.recipe: HALF: lack of control only
C.why_wrong: Jinny describes jealousy she cannot stop once it takes hold, which matches the first part of the claim, but she says nothing here about her love for Jack.

sources.what: Clyde Fitch, The Girl with the Green Eyes (Macmillan 1905; first produced at the Savoy Theatre, New York, 25 December 1902), Project Gutenberg eBook 19101; quotations copied from Acts II and IV (italic emphasis and stage directions removed, double hyphens set as dashes)

items.notes: Medium. Literature (play, 1902 first production per the edition's cast page). Fitch is used in no official item or live item. Two-part claim; C is the half-match that comes from the same speech as the key. Quotations verified against the Gutenberg text.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (takes her debts seriously; resolves to reveal all of them)
items.passage: Dolly Reforming Herself is a 1908 play by Henry Arthur Jones. Dolly Telfer has accumulated considerable debts by purchasing expensive clothing. Inspired by a New Year’s sermon, she resolves to abandon her extravagant habits. Conversing with her friend Renie, Dolly makes clear that she considers her debts genuinely serious and intends to disclose every one of them to her husband, Harry: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Dolly Reforming Herself most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Yesterday afternoon I thought I’d screw up my courage to go through the bills just to see where I was. My dear, I was paralysed!”
“Only bills! Only? Well, I’m going to show him every one this time. And what a lesson it shall be to me!”
“Harry? He made a dreadful fuss last time. And then I didn’t show him all.”
“I don’t care anything about my gray matter! I’ve quite made up my mind I won’t have any more bills!”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Dolly considers her debts serious, and she means to tell Harry about all of them. In choice B she protests “Only bills! Only?” when Renie makes light of them, which shows she takes them seriously, and she says “I’m going to show him every one this time,” which is her intention to disclose them all.

A.recipe: HALF: alarm at the debts, no intention to disclose
A.why_wrong: Dolly’s shock at her bills shows she takes them seriously, but she says nothing about showing them to Harry.

C.recipe: LURE: shows the bills to Harry, but in the past and only some
C.why_wrong: This line mentions showing the bills to Harry, but it recalls that last time she hid some of them; it does not express an intention to disclose them all.

D.recipe: HALF: a resolution about future bills, not disclosure
D.why_wrong: Dolly resolves to run up no more bills, but she says nothing about revealing her existing debts to Harry.

sources.what: Henry Arthur Jones, Dolly Reforming Herself: A Comedy in Four Acts (first produced at the Haymarket Theatre, 3 November 1908), Project Gutenberg eBook 27271; quotations copied from Act I (stage directions removed)

items.notes: Medium. Literature (play, 1908 first production per the edition's cast page; Act I is set on 1 January 1907, after Mr. Pilcher's New Year sermon). Jones is used in no official item or live item. Two-part claim; A and D are half-matches, C a lure on showing Harry the bills. A second play in the batch beside Fitch; the hard literary cell is a poem.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a conclusion that one mechanism (blocking sunlight) matters beyond another (cooling)
items.passage: Apples exposed to intense sunlight on hot days can develop sunburn, discolored patches on the skin that make the fruit difficult to sell. In orchards near Stellenbosch, South Africa, horticultural scientists Jiregna Gindaba and Stephanie Wand compared three protective techniques for Cripps’ Pink and Royal Gala apples. Overhead sprinklers cooled the fruit through evaporation, a sprayed-on film of kaolin clay reflected sunlight, and shade netting filtered it. The researchers concluded that techniques that reduce the sunlight reaching the fruit as well as its temperature prevent sunburn more effectively than techniques that only cool the fruit.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Gindaba and Wand’s conclusion?
options: On days when kaolin-coated fruit and sprinkler-cooled fruit stayed at similar temperatures, the kaolin-coated fruit developed less sunburn.
Fruit grown under shade netting developed less of the red blush color that buyers prefer than did the fruit in either of the other two treatments.
Royal Gala apples cooled by overhead sprinklers grew heavier, on average, than the Royal Gala apples in any of the other treatments did.
Fruit cooled by sprinklers developed no more sunburn than fruit under shade netting, even though the sprinklers did not block any sunlight.
items.explanation: Gindaba and Wand concluded that techniques that reduce “the sunlight reaching the fruit as well as its temperature” work better than techniques “that only cool the fruit.” If kaolin-coated fruit got less sunburn than sprinkler-cooled fruit on days when both were at similar temperatures, then the kaolin film’s advantage could not come from cooling alone; it must come from reducing sunlight, which supports the conclusion.

B.recipe: OFF: a different outcome (blush color), not sunburn
B.why_wrong: Reduced blush color concerns the fruit’s appearance at harvest, not how well the methods prevented sunburn.

C.recipe: OFF: a different outcome (fruit mass)
C.why_wrong: Heavier fruit under sprinklers says nothing about which method best prevented sunburn.

D.recipe: OPP: a cooling-only method as effective as a shading method
D.why_wrong: If sprinklers, which block no sunlight, prevented sunburn as well as shade netting, reducing sunlight would add nothing, which weakens the conclusion.

sources.what: Gindaba, Wand 2005, HortScience 40(3):592-596, Comparative Effects of Evaporative Cooling, Kaolin Particle Film, and Shade Net on Sunburn and Fruit Quality in Apples: Cripps' Pink and Royal Gala, Stellenbosch, South Africa; shade net, then kaolin, most effective against sunburn, evaporative cooling less effective; technologies that reduce irradiance as well as fruit temperature are more effective than those that only reduce fruit temperature; treatments reduced blush color; evaporative cooling increased fruit mass

items.notes: Medium. Life science (horticulture). The key holds temperature equal so that only sunlight differs (a controlled comparison). B and C are real results of the study on other outcomes. The abstract was read via OpenAlex (the publisher page blocks scripted access); Crossref confirms authors, journal and year. Year 2005 is inside the official range.

items.subtype: Data completion: two comparisons, one per year, showing a reversal of order
items.passage: Over the past two decades, automated teller machines (ATMs) have become scarcer in some countries, including several where payment by card is common. In others, where many residents previously had little access to financial services, ATMs have multiplied. According to the International Monetary Fund’s Financial Access Survey, these opposing trends between 2010 and 2020 even reversed the relative positions of some countries in the table: for example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
options: Norway had more ATMs per 100,000 adults than Sweden did in 2010, and Norway still had more ATMs per 100,000 adults than Sweden did in 2020.
India had fewer ATMs per 100,000 adults than Norway did in 2010 but more ATMs per 100,000 adults than Norway did in 2020.
China had fewer ATMs per 100,000 adults than Sweden did in 2010 but more ATMs per 100,000 adults than Sweden did in 2020.
Sweden had about 43 ATMs per 100,000 adults in 2010, but by 2020 it had only about 28 ATMs per 100,000 adults.

table.title: ATMs per 100,000 Adults in Four Countries, 2010 and 2020

items.explanation: The sentence calls for an example of countries whose “relative positions” were reversed between 2010 and 2020. China had 24.9 ATMs per 100,000 adults in 2010, fewer than Sweden’s 42.8, but 87.6 in 2020, more than Sweden’s 28.3, so the two countries traded places, as choice C states.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate sameness where a reversal is needed
A.why_wrong: Norway did have more ATMs per 100,000 adults than Sweden in both years, but an order that stays the same is not a reversal.

B.recipe: WDIR: the second comparison is false
B.why_wrong: India had fewer ATMs than Norway in 2010 (7.2 vs. 55.2) and still had fewer in 2020 (21.2 vs. 32.3), so the order did not reverse.

D.recipe: PART: accurate change for one country, no comparison
D.why_wrong: Sweden’s decline is read correctly, but a change in one country alone does not show two countries changing places.

sources.what: Automated teller machines (ATMs) per 100,000 adults, World Bank indicator FB.ATM.TOTL.P5 (source: IMF Financial Access Survey), values for China, India, Norway and Sweden in 2010 and 2020 checked via the World Bank API on 2026-10-27

items.notes: Medium. Economics/technology. Two comparisons per option, as in the medium models; distractors are sameness, a false second comparison, and a single-country change. ATMs appear in no other item.

items.subtype: Data description: contrasting trends (steady rise vs fluctuation) support a conclusion
items.passage: Battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles accounted for a rapidly growing proportion of new cars sold in Europe during the 2010s. Their growth, however, did not follow an identical trajectory everywhere. Reviewing International Energy Agency statistics, a student concludes that the electric share of new car sales in Sweden increased steadily from year to year, whereas in the Netherlands the share declined in some years and surged in others before reaching its highest level of the period in 2019.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the student’s conclusion?
options: From 2013 to 2019, the electric share of new car sales in the Netherlands was higher than the electric share in Sweden in every year shown.
Both the Netherlands and Sweden had a higher electric share of new car sales in 2019 than they had had in 2013.
Finland’s electric share of new car sales rose every year from 2013 to 2019 but was lower than Sweden’s in every one of those years.
Sweden’s share rose every year, whereas the Netherlands’ share fell from 2013 to 2015, jumped in 2016, fell in 2017, and peaked in 2019.

figure.title: Electric Cars as a Share of New Car Sales in Three Countries, 2013–2019
figure.y_axis: Share of new cars sold that were electric (%)
figure.description: Three lines for 2013 to 2019; y-axis 0 to 16 in steps of 2. Netherlands: about 5.5, 3.9, 3.5, 11, 6.4, 6.2, 15 (falls to 2015, jumps in 2016, drops in 2017, peaks in 2019). Sweden: about 0.5, 1.4, 2.4, 3.4, 5.1, 7.6, 11 (rises every year). Finland: about 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 1.2, 2.6, 4.7, 6.9 (rises every year, below Sweden throughout). The Netherlands is above Sweden from 2013 to 2017 and below it in 2018.

items.explanation: The student concludes that Sweden’s share “increased steadily from year to year,” while the Netherlands’ share “declined in some years and surged in others before reaching its highest level of the period in 2019.” The graph shows Sweden’s line rising every year, and the Netherlands’ line falling from about 5.5 percent in 2013 to about 3.5 percent in 2015, jumping to about 11 percent in 2016, falling to about 6 percent in 2017, and peaking at about 15 percent in 2019, as choice D states.

A.recipe: INACC: false in 2018
A.why_wrong: In 2018 the Netherlands’ share (about 6 percent) was lower than Sweden’s (about 8 percent), so the Netherlands was not higher in every year.

B.recipe: IRREL: accurate endpoints that hide the paths
B.why_wrong: Both countries did end higher than they began, but comparing only 2013 and 2019 says nothing about whether each country’s share rose steadily or fluctuated.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but about Finland
C.why_wrong: Finland’s steady rise is read correctly, but the conclusion contrasts Sweden with the Netherlands, so data about Finland do not support it.

sources.what: Share of new cars sold that are electric (battery-electric and plug-in hybrid), International Energy Agency Global EV Outlook 2025 via Our World in Data, values for the Netherlands, Sweden and Finland 2013-2019 checked 2026-10-27

items.notes: Medium. Technology/economics. Two-part trend (steady rise vs fluctuation); A is a false reading in one year, B accurate endpoints, C the right shape for the wrong country. Gridlines every 2 points make the 2016 jump and 2017 drop readable; no option depends on the 2017 to 2018 change (6.4 to 6.2). Electric car sales appear in no other item.

fixes: passage: the Netherlands half is now part of the student’s conclusion, as the explanation and key D already treated it

items.subtype: Data description: group comparison at two times (a gap that closes)
items.passage: The World Bank’s Global Findex surveys ask adults in numerous countries whether they hold an account with a bank, another financial institution, or a mobile money provider. Between 2011 and 2021, the proportion of Indian adults holding such an account more than doubled. Examining Findex data for India, a student concludes that during that decade, poorer adults went from being considerably less likely than wealthier adults to have an account to being approximately as likely.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the student’s conclusion?
options: The share of the richest 60 percent of adults with an account rose from about 41 percent in 2011 to about 60 percent in 2014 and to about 82 percent in 2017.
In 2011, about 27 percent of the poorest 40 percent had an account, against about 41 percent of the richest 60 percent, but by 2021 both shares were near 78 percent.
In every year shown, a larger share of the poorest 40 percent of adults than of the richest 60 percent of adults had an account at a bank or with a mobile money service.
The share of the poorest 40 percent of adults with an account rose from about 27 percent in 2011 to about 44 percent in 2014 and to about 78 percent in 2021.

figure.title: Share of Adults in India with an Account, by Income Group
figure.description: Paired bars for 2011, 2014, 2017 and 2021 (poorest 40% of adults, richest 60% of adults); y-axis 0 to 100 in steps of 10. Poorest 40% / richest 60%: 2011 about 27 / about 41; 2014 about 44 / about 60; 2017 about 77 / about 82; 2021 about 78 / about 77.

A.recipe: PART: one group over time, no comparison
A.why_wrong: The richest group’s rise is read correctly, but without the poorest group the choice cannot show how the gap between them changed.

C.recipe: INACC: true only in 2021

D.recipe: PART: the other group over time, no comparison

items.subtype: Quotation from a historian supports a student's claim about a person's priorities
items.passage: Paul Cuffe (1759–1817), the son of a Wampanoag mother and a formerly enslaved Ashanti father, established a prosperous shipping business in Westport, Massachusetts. In 1810 he sailed to Sierra Leone, a British colony settled largely by formerly enslaved people. In 1815 he transported nine families of free Black Americans to the colony. In a paper, a student argues that Cuffe believed the colony’s future depended more on its economic development than on the immigration of additional settlers from the United States.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by a historian would be the most effective evidence for the student to include in support of this claim?
options: “Cuffe concluded that Sierra Leone needed exportable crops and ships of its own; he valued the families he later brought from Massachusetts mainly for the skills they could teach.”
“Leaders of the American Colonization Society sought Cuffe’s advice because they hoped that his voyages could serve as a model for resettling large numbers of free Black Americans in Africa.”
“In his hometown of Westport, Cuffe helped found a school that admitted children of every race, and in 1813 he paid half the cost of a new meetinghouse for the town’s Quakers.”
“Cuffe learned seamanship on whaling voyages as a teenager and later built his own vessels in a boatyard on the Westport River, launching them into the Atlantic coastal trade.”
items.explanation: The student argues that Cuffe believed the colony’s future “depended more on its economic development than on the immigration of additional settlers from the United States.” Choice A says that Cuffe believed Sierra Leone needed “exportable crops and ships of its own” and that he valued the settlers he brought “mainly for the skills they could teach,” which places the economy first and the settlers second, as the claim states.

B.recipe: SUBJ: the colonization society’s view, not Cuffe’s
B.why_wrong: This quotation describes what the society’s leaders hoped for, large-scale resettlement, and says nothing about what Cuffe himself believed the colony needed.

C.recipe: OFF: his work in Westport
C.why_wrong: The school and the meetinghouse concern Cuffe’s life in Massachusetts, not his views about Sierra Leone.

D.recipe: LURE: commerce, but his own business, not the colony’s
D.why_wrong: The quotation concerns how Cuffe built his own shipping business; it says nothing about how he thought Sierra Leone’s future could be secured.

sources.what: Paul Cuffe: Black and Wampanoag businessman and sea captain; father an Ashanti man enslaved and later manumitted; whaling voyages as a youth; built ships on the Westport River and a shipping business along the Atlantic coast; founded a racially integrated school in Westport; donated half the money for the 1813 Westport meeting house; sailed to Sierra Leone in 1810 and concluded the settlers should increase exportable commodities and develop their own shipping; in 1815-16 transported nine families of free blacks to work with residents to develop the economy; declined to support the American Colonization Society, which had sought his advice

items.notes: Medium. History. Quotations are invented and attributed to an unnamed historian; their facts follow the source. Two components (economy first, settlers second); B is the society's view (wrong subject), D a commerce lure. Cuffe appears in no other item.

items.subtype: Data completion: read one named cell (value-only options)

To learn what the wolves of Montesinho Natural Park in northeastern Portugal eat, a team of researchers collected 85 wolf scats (droppings). They then recorded the percentage of scats that contained the remains of each kind of prey. According to the table, remains of wild boar were found in ______

options: 44% of the scats.
26% of the scats.
6% of the scats.
24% of the scats.

table.title: Prey Remains Found in Iberian Wolf Scats in Montesinho Natural Park

items.explanation: The table shows that remains of wild boar were found in 24 percent of the scats, so choice D correctly completes the statement.

A.recipe: WGRP: the value for roe deer
A.why_wrong: 44 percent is the share of scats containing roe deer, not wild boar.

B.recipe: WGRP: the value for red deer
B.why_wrong: 26 percent is the share of scats containing red deer, not wild boar.

C.recipe: WGRP: the value for cats

Iberian wolf diet in Montesinho Natural Park, northeast Portugal: 85 scats collected between November 2017 and August 2019; frequency of occurrence roe deer 44%, red deer 26%, wild boar 24%, domestic/wild cat 6%, domestic goat and stone marten 5%; Iberian wolf declined in Portugal through the 20th century
