items.subtype: Data completion, reverse lookup (the Soviet rover that landed in 1973, then its distance)
items.passage: Since 1970, robotic rovers built by the Soviet Union, China, and India have explored the lunar surface, each one steered remotely by operators on Earth. A student comparing these vehicles notes that the Soviet rover that landed on the Moon in 1973 traveled ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: 10,500 meters.
39,000 meters.
115 meters.
101 meters.

table.title: Four Rovers That Have Operated on the Moon

items.explanation: The table shows two Soviet rovers. The one that landed in 1973 is Lunokhod 2, and the table shows that it traveled 39,000 meters.

A.recipe: WGRP: the other Soviet rover
A.why_wrong: 10,500 meters is the distance traveled by Lunokhod 1, the Soviet rover that landed in 1970, not 1973.

C.recipe: WGRP: a Chinese rover
C.why_wrong: 115 meters is the distance traveled by Yutu, a Chinese rover that landed in 2013.

D.recipe: WGRP: an Indian rover
D.why_wrong: 101 meters is the distance traveled by Pragyan, an Indian rover that landed in 2023.

sources.what: Wikipedia, List of rovers on extraterrestrial bodies, lunar rovers: Lunokhod 1 (Luna 17, USSR) landed 17 November 1970, 10.5 km; Lunokhod 2 (Luna 21, USSR) landed 15 January 1973, 39 km, farthest distance traveled on the Moon; Yutu (Chang'e 3, CNSA) landed 14 December 2013, 114.8 m; Pragyan (Chandrayaan-3, ISRO) landed 23 August 2023, 101.4 m. Yutu-2 is left out because its distance is given only as of a date while it was still operating.

items.notes: Easy reverse lookup (CB 1.37, 1.43 style): the student must find the 1973 row among two Soviet rovers. Yutu's 114.8 m and Pragyan's 101.4 m are rounded to whole meters.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a causal claim (snails reduce slug damage): one-step operationalization with the right comparison
items.passage: The Spanish slug (Arion vulgaris), an invasive species, has spread across much of Europe in recent decades, damaging crops and ornamental plants. Daniel Dörler and colleagues grew lettuce in containers holding Spanish slugs alone, Roman snails (Helix pomatia) alone, or both species together. They were testing an idea popular among gardeners: that the presence of the Roman snail, a large native species, reduces the destruction Spanish slugs cause.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the gardeners’ idea?
options: Roman snails ate less lettuce for their body weight than Spanish slugs did when each species was kept alone in a container.
Spanish slugs ate more lettuce in containers that were watered every day than in containers that were watered only once every three days.
Roman snails ate almost none of the eggs laid by Spanish slugs when the snails were offered the eggs as food.
Spanish slugs that shared a container with Roman snails ate less lettuce for their body weight than slugs kept without snails did.
items.explanation: The gardeners’ idea is that “the presence of the Roman snail, a large native species, reduces the destruction Spanish slugs cause.” If slugs that shared a container with Roman snails ate less lettuce for their body weight than slugs kept without snails, the snails’ presence would have reduced the slugs’ damage to the lettuce, which is exactly what the idea predicts.

A.recipe: OFF: compares the two species instead of slugs with and without snails
A.why_wrong: This shows only that snails eat less than slugs do; it says nothing about whether having snails around changes how much the slugs eat.

B.recipe: OFF: a different variable (watering)
B.why_wrong: How watering affects the slugs’ feeding has nothing to do with whether Roman snails reduce the damage slugs do.

C.recipe: OPP: rules out one way snails could control slugs
C.why_wrong: If the snails hardly ever ate slug eggs, they would not be reducing the number of slugs that way, so this would, if anything, weaken the gardeners’ idea.

sources.what: Dorler, Dorn, Widhalm, Horacek, Heigl, Euteneuer et al. 2021, PeerJ 9: e11309, Experimental indications of gardeners' anecdotes that snails interfere with invasive slugs: the invasive Spanish slug (Arion vulgaris) has spread across Europe and outcompetes native slugs and snails; a popular anecdote suggests promoting Roman snails (Helix pomatia) because they control A. vulgaris; mesocosm experiment with lettuce, Arion only, Helix only and both; herbivory per body mass lower in mixed mesocosms than Arion-only ones; three of 200 Arion eggs eaten by Helix (abstract, Europe PMC PMC8121057)

items.notes: Easy one-step item. The key is close to the paper's result, stated as a hypothetical; C states the paper's real egg result and is wrong because it weakens. Dorler spelled Dörler in the passage.

items.subtype: Quotation from a historian supports a claim about influence (social work shaped the activities of the organization she organized)
items.passage: In the 1920s, Filipino teacher Josefa Llanes Escoda earned a master’s degree in social work in New York and then returned home to direct relief work in rural communities for the Red Cross in the Philippines. In 1939 she went to the United States for training in girl scouting, and in 1940 she organized the Girl Scouts of the Philippines. A history student claims that Escoda’s experience in social work shaped the activities of the new organization.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by a historian would be the most effective evidence for the student to include in support of this claim?
options: “On the night before the 1937 vote that decided whether Filipino women would gain the right to vote, Escoda spoke on the radio in Ilocano, the language of her home province, urging listeners to support the measure.”
“When President Manuel L. Quezon signed its charter in May 1940, the Girl Scouts of the Philippines had about 1,000 members, and by December 1941 it had about 3,000.”

“When Japanese forces occupied the Philippines during World War II, members of the Girl Scouts of the Philippines raised funds for relief work and helped bring food, clothing, and medicine to prisoners of war.”
“While studying in New York, Escoda paid many of her expenses by working in offices and caring for children, and she gave paid lectures about the Philippines to American audiences.”
items.explanation: The student claims that Escoda’s experience in social work, which included directing “relief work in rural communities,” shaped the activities of the Girl Scouts of the Philippines. Choice C shows such an activity: during World War II, members of the organization “raised funds for relief work and helped bring food, clothing, and medicine to prisoners of war,” the same kind of relief work Escoda had directed as a social worker.

A.recipe: OFF: her suffrage campaign, not the organization's activities
A.why_wrong: This shows Escoda campaigning for women’s right to vote, but it says nothing about what the Girl Scouts of the Philippines did, so it cannot show that her social work shaped that organization’s activities.

B.recipe: TRAP: about the organization, but its size rather than its activities
B.why_wrong: This describes how many members the Girl Scouts of the Philippines had, not what those members did, so it gives no evidence that Escoda’s social work shaped the organization’s activities.

D.recipe: OFF: her student jobs and lectures
D.why_wrong: This describes how Escoda supported herself as a student in New York; it concerns neither her relief work nor the activities of the organization she later organized.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Josefa Llanes Escoda: Filipino teacher and social worker; New York School of Social Work, master's degree in social work from Columbia University (1925); paid expenses with office work and baby-sitting and gave paid lectures about the Philippines; field secretary of the Philippine Chapter of the American Red Cross 1926 to 1929, managing civilian relief in rural communities; spoke in Ilocano on radio station KZRM on the eve of the 30 April 1937 women's suffrage plebiscite; trained in girl scouting in the United States in 1939; Quezon signed the Girl Scouts of the Philippines charter on 26 May 1940 (1,000 Girl Scouts), about 3,000 by December 1941; during the occupation the Girl Scouts provided funds for social work and relief to prisoners of war and, with the NFWC, clothing, food and medicine (page fetched). Historian quotations are invented, unattributed, and consistent with these facts.

items.notes: Reviewer replaced the subject: Jovita Idár, La Crónica and the League of Mexican Women are an official Transitions item (cb 2b5f4bdc). Easy T3: the key is the only quotation about what the organization's members did; B is about the organization but only its size. All four quotations come from an unnamed historian; no words are put in the mouth of Escoda or any named person, and her own wartime message is not used.

fixes: replaced the subject: Jovita Idár, La Crónica and the League of Mexican Women are an official Transitions item (cb 2b5f4bdc); new subject Josefa Llanes Escoda and the Girl Scouts of the Philippines, checked on Wikipedia, claim appended and the old one withdrawn
all four quotations come from an unnamed historian; no words put in a named person's mouth
key letter C kept

items.subtype: Literary quotation, single trait (the Lithuanian is stubbornly determined)
items.passage: “If Not Higher” is a short story by I.L. Peretz, translated from Yiddish in 1906 by Helena Frank. The narrator presents a skeptical Lithuanian visitor as stubbornly determined to learn where the town’s Rebbe (religious leader) goes early on Friday mornings: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from “If Not Higher” most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “He confessed afterwards, did the Lithuanian, that when he found himself alone with the Rebbe terror took hold of him.”
“But a Lithuanian is dogged. He quivers and quakes like a fish—but he does not budge.”
“The Rebbe keeps to the street side, and walks in the shadow of the houses.”
“Behind the town stands a little wood. The Rebbe, long life to him, enters it. He walks on thirty or forty paces, and then he stops beside a small tree.”
items.explanation: The claim is that the narrator presents the Lithuanian as stubbornly determined. In choice B the narrator calls him “dogged” and adds that although he “quivers and quakes like a fish,” he “does not budge.” The Lithuanian is frightened, yet he holds his ground, which shows his stubborn determination.

A.recipe: HALF: his fear without his persistence
A.why_wrong: This quotation shows that “terror took hold of” the Lithuanian, but it does not show him holding his ground in spite of that fear, so it does not show his determination.

C.recipe: SUBJ: describes the Rebbe, not the Lithuanian
C.why_wrong: This quotation describes how the Rebbe walks through the town; it says nothing about the Lithuanian.

D.recipe: OFF: setting and the Rebbe’s actions
D.why_wrong: This quotation describes the wood behind the town and where the Rebbe stops; it says nothing about the Lithuanian’s determination.

sources.what: I.L. Peretz, Stories and Pictures, translated from the Yiddish by Helena Frank (Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society of America, 1906), story I, If Not Higher. Quotations copied verbatim (Gutenberg -- rendered as an em dash). The preface dates the stories only broadly (written 1875 to 1900), so no year of first publication is given.

items.notes: Easy single-trait claim. Left out on purpose: The Lithuanian trembles, but he persists, and Another in his place would have dozed... he learned a whole treatise of the Talmud by heart, which would also show determination.

fixes: the Rebbe vanishes early on Friday mornings in the story, not each morning: passage corrected
all four quotations verbatim (Gutenberg 37242)

items.subtype: Data completion, a sharp rise in one series among four (example of a stated trend)
items.passage: Since the late 2010s, Saudi Arabia has introduced a series of reforms affecting women, including lifting its longstanding ban on women driving in 2018. During the same period, the share of Saudi women in the labor force (the percentage of women aged 15 and older who are either employed or looking for work) increased considerably, as estimates from the International Labour Organization show. According to the graph, for instance, the labor force participation rate for women in Saudi Arabia ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
options: rose from about 20% in 2017 to about 34% in 2022.
stayed at about 30% from 2015 to 2022.
fell from about 23% in 2016 to about 15% in 2022.
stayed below 17% in every year shown, from 2015 to 2022.

figure.title: Labor Force Participation Rate for Women in Four Countries, 2015–2022
figure.y_axis: Women aged 15 and older in the labor force (%)
figure.description: Four lines at each year from 2015 to 2022; y-axis 0 to 30 percent in steps of 10, with the plot extending to about 38. Saudi Arabia: about 22, 23, 20, 22, 24, 29, 34, 34 (a sharp rise after 2017). Oman: about 30, 30, 31, 30, 30, 29, 30, 31 (nearly flat). Egypt: about 23, 23, 22, 18, 16, 15, 16, 15 (a decline). Jordan: about 14, 15, 17, 15, 14, 15, 14, 14 (nearly flat and lowest). Saudi Arabia rises above Oman in 2021.

items.explanation: The text says that the share of Saudi women in the labor force “increased considerably,” so the example must show a large increase for Saudi Arabia. The graph shows that Saudi Arabia’s rate rose from about 20% in 2017 to about 34% in 2022, as choice A states.

B.recipe: WGRP: Oman’s nearly flat line
B.why_wrong: The rate that stayed at about 30% is Oman’s; Saudi Arabia’s rate rose from about 20% to about 34%.

C.recipe: WGRP: Egypt’s declining line
C.why_wrong: The rate that fell from about 23% to about 15% is Egypt’s, and a decline would not illustrate an increase in any case.

D.recipe: WGRP: Jordan’s low, flat line
D.why_wrong: The rate that stayed below 17% is Jordan’s; Saudi Arabia’s rate was above 17% in every year shown.

sources.what: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Labor force participation rate, female (% of female population ages 15+) (modeled ILO estimate), SL.TLF.CACT.FE.ZS, 2015-2022 (API fetched): Saudi Arabia 21.6, 22.9, 19.9, 21.8, 24.4, 29.3, 34.2, 34.1; Oman 29.6 ... 30.8; Egypt 22.8 ... 15.2; Jordan 13.6 ... 13.9
Saudi Arabia lifted its ban on women driving on 24 June 2018 (Wikipedia, Women to drive movement)

items.notes: Easy trend item modeled on 1.10 (one series rises sharply among four; wrong options give the other series' patterns). The passage claims only that the two happened in the same period, not that one caused the other.

fixes: no change: series match World Bank SL.TLF.CACT.FE.ZS 2015 to 2022
